one_liner: Go BLAKE3 package with avo-generated AVX-512/AVX2 assembly; about 4-8x its own pure-Go path on 64 KiB inputs.
what_it_does: A Go implementation of BLAKE3 (import path lukechampine.com/blake3). It offers a hash.Hash Hasher from New(size, key), one-shot Sum256/Sum512, DeriveKey, a seekable XOF OutputReader, and Bao verified-streaming encode/decode in the bao subpackage. On amd64 it picks AVX-512 or AVX2 kernels at init; every other architecture, arm64 included, runs the pure-Go compressor. It satisfies hash.Hash, but the Go standard library has no BLAKE3, so there is no stdlib call it replaces.
how_it_is_fast: BLAKE3 cuts the input into 1 KiB chunks that are leaves of a binary Merkle tree, so independent chunks can be compressed side by side in SIMD lanes. compressChunksAVX512 hashes 16 chunks per call (MaxSIMD = 16, 'AVX-512 vectors can store 16 words') and compressChunksAVX2 hashes 8, both with all 7 rounds inlined; an AVX2 kernel merges parent nodes 8 at a time, and XOF output compresses 16 successive counter values of the root node at once. The assembly is generated by Go programs using mmcloughlin/avo, not written by hand. Since v1.4.0 (February 2025) Write also compresses each power-of-two subtree (eigentree), and each 16 KiB group inside it, in its own goroutine, and large XOF reads are split across up to runtime.NumCPU goroutines.
when_to_use: Hashing large buffers or streams (tens of KiB and up) in Go on x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512: in the author's 2020 run, Sum256 of 64 KiB reached 4.0 GB/s (AVX-512) and 2.1 GB/s (AVX2) against 0.49 GB/s in pure Go.
Long XOF output (key streams, deterministic random bytes) on x86-64, where one SIMD call produces 16 output blocks (1 KiB): 4.2 GB/s vs 0.53 GB/s in pure Go.
Content addressing or verified streaming that needs Bao encode/decode, slices or chunk groups in pure Go without cgo.
Batch jobs that hash a few very large inputs and are glad to use every core per hash (v1.4.0 and later parallelize Write and XOF).
when_not_to_use: Inputs up to about 1 KiB (keys, short messages): there is no single-block assembly, so 64 B and 1 KiB inputs run the same pure-Go code on every CPU (README 'Shortcomings'; issue #21 still open).
arm64 (Apple Silicon, Graviton) or x86 without AVX2: pure Go only, with no NEON or SSE4.1 kernels.
Servers already saturating their cores with many concurrent hashes: since v1.4.0 every Write longer than 1 KiB allocates a slice and starts goroutines, and there is no single-threaded option.
Decisions that need current numbers: the README figures come from August 2020 code, before the 2021 avo regeneration, the April 2024 VZEROUPPER fix for the AVX2 routines and the 2025 goroutine path.
Builds pinned to v1.4.0: that release is retracted because it returned wrong hashes for some split writes.

integration.form: module (Go package lukechampine.com/blake3, with guts and bao subpackages)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.22 (go.mod; the code uses the min builtin and range over an int)
integration.platforms: any Go target; assembly only on amd64 (AVX2 or AVX512F detected at init, with a sysctl fallback for AVX-512 on darwin); arm64 and other architectures run pure Go
integration.thread_safety: not documented; a Hasher is a mutable hash.Hash for one goroutine at a time, while Sum256/Sum512 copy a default hasher that is never mutated and can be called concurrently; Write and XOF reads fan out to goroutines internally
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the baseline is the package's own pure-Go path, chosen automatically on CPUs without AVX2; there is no build tag or setting that forces a path, and the API is hash.Hash plus io.Reader/io.Seeker for XOF output

gotchas: Benchmark labelling: BenchmarkWrite streams b.N KiB through io.CopyN, so each Write call receives io.Copy's 32 KiB buffer, and the 2020 BenchmarkXOF read through ioutil.Discard's 8 KiB buffer. The ns/op figures are per KiB streamed, not the cost of 1 KiB writes or reads. The 64 B and 1 KiB rows are identical in all three listings (120 ns and 2229 ns, MB/s to the hundredth), so they were pasted rather than re-run. Neither the 2020 nor the current code has a flag or build tag that selects AVX2 or pure Go on an AVX-512 machine, so producing those listings meant editing the source. The labelled CPU (i5-7600K, no AVX-512) cannot have run the AVX-512 listing.

The current code is not the measured code. Write and Sum on inputs over 1 KiB have used goroutines since v1.4.0 (the 2020 blake3.go has none). CompressEigentree starts one goroutine per 16 KiB group with no cap; only XOF output is capped at runtime.NumCPU. A single Write with a 512 MiB subtree starts 32,768 goroutines (derived from the code). Re-running the benchmarks today on a multi-core machine measures parallel throughput, which cannot be compared with single-threaded BLAKE3 figures.

v1.4.0 (2025-02-24) is retracted in go.mod. Its parallel Write consumed a partly filled buffer greedily, so Sum depended on how the input was split across Write calls; 83c0fac (v1.4.1, 2025-05-08) fixed it, and TestSplitWrite now checks every split point of a 2 KiB input.

New(size, key) returns no error: a key shorter than 32 bytes panics, and a longer key is silently truncated to its first 32 bytes. OutputReader.Seek panics on an invalid whence, which the maintainer kept on purpose (issue #16).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against zeebo/blake3 (AVX-512, AVX2, SSE4.1 and NEON kernels, with an assembly gain even at 64 B in its own tables), pick this package for Bao verified streaming, a seekable XOF, or built-in multi-core hashing of large inputs on amd64, and zeebo/blake3 for arm64, SSE4.1-only CPUs or small inputs. Use cespare/xxhash when a non-cryptographic hash is enough.
verified_claims_summary: Author's go test -bench output from August 2020, with no Go version or flags, on a CPU labelled '2020 MacBook Air (i5-7600K @ 3.80GHz)', a label the AVX-512 listing contradicts. Sum256 of 64 KiB took 16.2 us with AVX-512 (4.0 GB/s), 31.1 us with AVX2 (2.1 GB/s) and 133.5 us in pure Go (0.49 GB/s), about 8.2x and 4.3x; streaming Write and XOF throughput gained 4-8x, and 64 B and 1 KiB inputs gained nothing. The code was single-threaded then, and the baseline is the same package's pure-Go compressor built by gc.
status_note: Stale since v1.4.1 (2025-05-08), with 425 stars and an MIT licence; it is pure Go apart from generated amd64 assembly and small enough to vendor, but its README benchmarks date from August 2020 and do not describe the current multi-goroutine code.
